beats: Hook: GPT-3 read 2 tokens for every parameter; Llama 3 70B read 215. Why overfeed a model? (line_recipe_reading_stacks)
A model is a recipe of proportions, not only an architecture (line_recipe_card_stand, line_knob_board).
Chinchilla: ~20 tokens per parameter is compute-optimal for training (slide 33; callback to L01-01's 70B beats 280B) (line_recipe_chinchilla_books, line_balance).
But inference is the bill that keeps coming: pay up front in training for a smaller model that is cheaper to serve every day (her words, slide 33) (line_recipe_dogs_bowls, line_receipt).
Deep or wide: d_model / n_layer about 100-200; layers run one after another, width runs in parallel, so wider means lower latency (slide 34) (line_recipe_relay_vs_row).
FFN width: 4 x d_model for plain activations, about 8/3 for gated ones (slide 35; callback to L02-02) (line_tap_glass).
Batch size: millions of tokens per step (Llama 3 4M-16M+); bigger batches mean fewer steps for the same compute and more machines at work (slide 36) (line_recipe_cookie_tray).

Pitfall: past the critical batch size a bigger tray stops buying speed (line_recipe_tray_stuck); the good news (her words): it depends on the target loss, not the model size, so a small model can find it first (line_recipe_test_kitchen); in practice teams go past it anyway, paying overhead to cut months to days.
Takeaway: four ratios on one card; next lecture: how training is spread across thousands of GPUs (L04).
